newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Top Russian says no econ. tie to Romania NATO bid.
newsitem.headline: Top Russian says no econ. tie to Romania NATO bid.

text.p: Russia, which opposes NATO plans to admit ex-communist members, has no intention of using economic levers to hinder Romania's drive to join the Atlantic alliance, a senior Russian official said on Friday.

"Russia does not link Romania's integration or non-integration into NATO to economic matters," Gennady Seleznyov, chairman of Russia's lower house of parliament, the State Duma, told Reuters at the end of a two-day visit.
"We have concrete economic projects with Romania. They will be observed."
Romania's energy and petrochemical sectors are heavily dependent on imports of Russian gas and raw materials.
Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are favourites to be admitted at a July NATO summit in Madrid but Romania and Slovenia have recently improved their chances.
Senior Western officials say Romania's case has strengthened since centrists committed to market reforms ousted ex-communists in elections last November.
They also praise Romania's conclusion of a treaty with Hungary burying differences over territory and ethnic minorities and renewed efforts to sign a similar accord with neighbouring Ukraine.
Though a Warsaw Pact member in the Communist era, Romania frequently deviated in its policies, refusing, for instance, to take part in the 1968 Soviet-led invasion of Czechoslovakia.
Bucharest was never a reliable ally for Moscow and wants now to improve ties, which remained cool even after the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union.
At a news conference, Seleznyov said he had reiterated Moscow's strong opposition to NATO expansion in talks with Romania's new leaders.
"I told them that NATO is not a peace dove but a military bloc which should have a potential enemy," he said. "Nobody was able to tell me who Romania's enemies are."
Seleznyov also said he expected Moscow and Bucharest to resume talks on a long-delayed post-communist treaty.

But he ruled out any reference in the document to secret protocols in the 1939 Nazi-Soviet pact under which Romania lost lands to the Kremlin, which have since become part of post-Soviet Ukraine and Moldova.
Treaty talks with Russia -- as with Ukraine and Moldova -- are stalled over Bucharest's demand for public acknowledgement of its lost territory.
"Such references are not acceptable. Why should we invent now a series of problems for Ukraine and Moldova and find solutions to problems that no longer exist?," he said.
